analysis.one_liner: Ends a range of tax breaks and royalty relief for oil and gas companies.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor in the Senate and died in the Finance Committee when the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have stripped away a long list of tax advantages enjoyed by oil and gas companies: deductions for drilling costs, a percentage depletion allowance, a credit for enhanced oil recovery, tax preferences for the largest integrated oil companies, and royalty relief for drilling in the Gulf of Mexico and offshore Alaska that had been enacted in the 2005 energy law. The revenue those preferences forgo would otherwise have gone to the Treasury, which is funded by ordinary taxpayers. The bill was introduced by Senator John Kerry in January 2007, sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, ordinary taxpayers would have benefited in two ways: the federal government would collect more tax revenue from oil and gas companies instead of leaving those preferences in place, and the tax code would treat energy companies like other businesses rather than giving them specialized deductions. Taxpayers in Gulf Coast and Alaska coastal areas also would have gained indirectly, since the bill ended royalty relief that let companies drill on federal lands and waters while paying reduced or no royalties to the government.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary taxpayers and the federal Treasury

how_it_helps.text: It terminates three long-standing oil and gas tax preferences: the deduction for intangible drilling and development costs, the percentage depletion allowance, and the enhanced oil recovery credit [S2][S3].

It repeals a series of Energy Policy Act of 2005 provisions that benefited the industry, including deep-water royalty relief, Gulf of Mexico natural gas production incentives, Alaska offshore royalty suspension, accelerated depreciation for electric transmission and natural gas lines, expensing of refinery property, and two-year amortization of geological and geophysical costs [S2][S3].

It targets the largest integrated oil companies specifically: companies producing at least 500,000 barrels of crude a day with over $1 billion in gross receipts must revalue their LIFO inventories under a formula set in the bill, increasing their taxable income, and it limits foreign tax credits and deferrals for oil and gas companies operating abroad [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would bear the cost: they would lose decades-old tax deductions, credits, and expensing provisions, the largest integrated oil companies would face a one-time revaluation of their inventories that increases taxable income, and companies drilling offshore would lose royalty relief and production incentives. To the extent the industry passed some of these costs into fuel prices, consumers could bear part of it.

drawbacks.text: Some of the repealed provisions were designed to encourage domestic energy investment — expensing of refinery property, accelerated depreciation of electric transmission lines, and incentives for Gulf of Mexico gas production — and ending them could slow that investment [S3].
The bill terminated the breaks immediately upon enactment, with no phase-out, which critics of such proposals argue could disrupt drilling and production plans already underway.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit would be a more even tax code: oil and gas companies would pay the same effective taxes other businesses pay, recovering revenue from an industry that was enjoying both large profits and specialized tax preferences [S2][S3]. The strongest good-faith objection is that some of these breaks exist to encourage drilling, refinery construction, and pipeline investment, and ending them could modestly slow domestic energy production or raise costs at the margin for consumers. The bill also would have been applied immediately upon enactment, giving companies no transition time to adjust. The bill did nothing to address energy prices directly — its purpose was tax fairness and revenue, and any benefit to consumers would have been indirect.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Senator Kerry on January 22, 2007 and was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S5].
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].
Not a single senator signed on as a cosponsor during the two-year Congress [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies, which kept every tax break and royalty provision the bill would have repealed, and the senators who faced no record of voting on them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies, which kept their tax breaks

for.name: Sen. John F. Kerry
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 22, 2007 to repeal oil and gas tax preferences and 2005 energy law royalty relief.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on January 22, 2007 and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held and no other senator cosponsored the bill, so no partisan split is visible in the record [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill is aimed squarely at them: loss of drilling-cost deductions and foreign tax credit and deferral benefits, plus a mandatory revaluation of LIFO inventories that would raise their taxable income for 2006 [S2][S3].
Lose the percentage depletion allowance, intangible drilling cost deduction, and enhanced oil recovery credit — decades-old tax preferences that reduce the cost of drilling [S2][S3].
Lose royalty relief and production incentives in the Gulf of Mexico and offshore Alaska that let them drill on public waters while paying reduced or no royalties to the federal government [S2][S3].
Lose temporary expensing of refinery equipment, and the small-refiner exception to the oil depletion limitation is closed off [S3].

industries.industry: Electric transmission and natural gas utilities
industries.note: Lose accelerated depreciation of electric transmission property, natural gas distribution lines, and gathering lines, which had shortened the tax life of these investments [S2][S3].
